title: Electricity

hints: Recall that current in a filament causes heating, so consider how filament temperature changes when current decreases and how resistance of a metal depends on temperature due to lattice ion vibration and electron collisions.
walkthrough: B1: Temperature of filament decreases as heating effect is reduced, so resistance decreases.
teacher_walkthrough: Resistance of a metal filament depends on temperature. Current produces a heating effect with power $P = I^2 R$, so a smaller current gives less heating and the filament temperature falls. In a metal, higher temperature means greater amplitude of vibration of lattice ions and more frequent collisions with conduction electrons, giving higher resistance. Therefore when temperature falls, collision rate falls and resistance decreases.
common_pitfalls: Stating resistance increases because lower current is assumed to mean higher resistance from $R = V/I$ without considering that $V$ also changes and that filament is non-ohmic.
Omitting the temperature link and only stating resistance decreases, which does not earn the explanation mark.

hints: Recall the definition of resistance linking potential difference $V$ and current, and rearrange to make current the subject in terms of $V$ and $R$.
walkthrough: A1: current = V / R from $R = V/I$.
teacher_walkthrough: Resistance is defined by $$R = \frac{V}{I}$$ where $V$ is potential difference across the wire and $I$ is current. Rearranging to make current the subject: $$I = \frac{V}{R}$$ This is the current in terms of $V$ and $R$.
common_pitfalls: Inverting the relation to give $IR/V$ or $VR$, confusing subject of $R = V/I$.
Introducing $N$, $e$ or $L$ unnecessarily in this part, although only $V$ and $R$ are needed.

hints: Start from the drift speed relation $I = nAve$ where $n$ is number density of free electrons, $A$ is cross-sectional area and $v$ is drift speed, and identify that $n$ must be found from total number $N$ divided by volume $AL$.
Substitute $n = N/(AL)$ into $v = I/(nAe)$ and then substitute $I = V/R$ from (b)(i), then cancel $A$ to leave $v$ in terms of $V$, $L$, $R$, $N$ and $e$.
walkthrough: C1: Use $I = nAve$ with $n = N/(AL)$ where $AL$ is volume.
teacher_walkthrough: Current is related to drift speed by $$I = nAv e$$ where $n$ is number of free electrons per unit volume, $A$ is cross-sectional area, $v$ is average drift speed. Rearranged: $$v = \frac{I}{nAe}$$ Number density $n$ is total number divided by volume. Volume of cylindrical wire is area times length: $$\text{volume} = AL$$ so $$n = \frac{N}{AL}$$ Substitute $n$ and $I = V/R$ from (b)(i): $$v = \frac{V/R}{\left(N/AL\right)Ae}$$ The area $A$ cancels: $$v = \frac{V/R}{Ne/L}$$ $$v = \frac{VL}{RNe}$$ with units of $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
common_pitfalls: Using $N$ directly as number density $n$, forgetting to divide by volume $AL$, leading to missing factor $L$.
Failing to cancel cross-sectional area $A$ correctly or introducing unknown $A$ into final expression when question requires only $e, L, N, R, V$.

hints: Recall that average time to travel length $L$ at constant drift speed $v$ is $t = L/v$, or equivalently total charge $Ne$ divided by current $I$, then substitute $v$ from (b)(ii) or $I$ from (b)(i).
walkthrough: A1: $t = L/v = L/(VL/RNe) = RNe/V$, or $t = Q/I = Ne/(V/R) = RNe/V$.
teacher_walkthrough: Time for uniform motion is distance divided by speed: $$t = \frac{L}{v}$$ Substitute $v = VL/(RNe)$ from (b)(ii): $$t = \frac{L}{VL/(RNe)}$$ Invert denominator: $$t = \frac{L RNe}{VL}$$ Cancel $L$: $$t = \frac{RNe}{V}$$ Equivalently, total charge passing is $Q = Ne$ and $t = Q/I = Ne/(V/R)$ gives the same result, with units of $\text{s}$.
common_pitfalls: Inverting $t = L/v$ to $v/L$, giving $V/(RNe)$ instead of $RNe/V$.
Confusing total charge $Ne$ with elementary charge $e$ alone when using $t = Q/I$.
